claims.text: Codex is a cloud-based coding agent powered by codex-1, a version of OpenAI o3 optimized for software engineering.
Each Codex agent runs in its own cloud container, which is preloaded with the user's code and a user-defined development environment including dependencies, configuration, and tooling.
After environment setup, internet access is disabled and the model trajectory begins in the original Codex cloud design.
Within its container, Codex can read and edit files and execute commands including tests, linters, and type checkers.
Codex is trained to provide verifiable evidence of its actions through citations of terminal logs and files, so users can validate its work.
When a Codex task is complete, users can inspect results, request refinements, or export the diff by converting it into a GitHub pull request or copying it for local testing.

Codex Cloud (Legacy) uses a two-phase runtime: the setup phase can access the network to install specified dependencies, then the agent phase runs offline by default unless internet access is enabled for that environment.
Codex reads AGENTS.md files before doing any work.
Codex cloud agents run in an isolated OpenAI-hosted container with network access disabled by default, which prevents interaction with the user's host system or data outside the designated workspace.
Disabling network access by default is intended to significantly reduce the risk of prompt injection, data exfiltration, and the agent connecting to malicious external resources.

Codex cloud originally launched with a strictly network-disabled sandbox; users then asked for the flexibility to choose the level of internet connectivity, for example to install or update dependencies missed during environment configuration.
Users decide per project which sites, if any, the Codex cloud agent may access, including a custom allowlist or denylist, or internet access at large.

OpenAI warns that enabling internet access can introduce prompt injection, leaked credentials, and use of code with license restrictions, and advises limiting access to trusted domains and safe HTTP methods.
An allowed domain in Agent Security does not override a restriction in the Codex Cloud environment's internet settings; the two apply separately.

With self-hosted sandboxes, OpenAI runs the agent harness while the customer runs `codex exec-server` in their environment, which executes shell commands, reads and writes files, and uses local MCP servers.

The self-hosted executor connects outbound over WebSocket (wss://codex-cloud-environments.chatgpt.com) after registering with api.openai.com using an environment ID and a restricted API key; all connections are outbound and it reconnects if dropped.
Automatic review with review: "auto_review" in self-hosted sandboxes applies a permission profile with a workspace-write baseline and restricted network access.
Internally, OpenAI does not run Codex with open-ended outbound access; its managed network policy allows expected destinations, blocks unwanted ones, and requires approval for unfamiliar domains.

OpenAI's Auto-review mode sends the planned action and recent context to an auto-approval subagent that can approve low-risk actions, or high-risk ones with sufficient user authorization, instead of interrupting the user.
OpenAI uses rules so common benign engineering commands run outside the sandbox without approval while specific dangerous commands are blocked or require approval.

Codex supports OpenTelemetry log export for user prompts, tool approval decisions, tool execution results, MCP server usage, and network proxy allow/deny events, which OpenAI also uses to track internal adoption and tune rollout.

Through August 2025 the average OpenAI worker spent less than 10% of their tokens on Codex; by 2026 Codex accounted for more than 85% of the average worker's output tokens and 99.8% of weekly output tokens generated within OpenAI.
By May 2026, 80.6% of sampled OpenAI users made at least one Codex request estimated to exceed 30 minutes of human work, 70.2% exceeded one hour, and 25.6% exceeded eight hours.
On June 11, 2026, the median OpenAI employee had Codex turns running for 2.5 hours, while 99th-percentile users ran about 71 hours of agent turns per day, implying several concurrent agents.
99th-percentile OpenAI users increased cumulative daily Codex runtime by nearly 88% since April 7, 2026.
